reasoning: The core problem — whether independently developed LLMs converge on the same Schelling/focal point in classic coordination games and how this compares to humans — is directly and recently addressed. The arXiv paper "Tacit Coordination of Large Language Models" (2601.22184) tests heterogeneous independent open-source models (Llama, Qwen, GPT-oss) on classic focal-point games drawn from human experiments (Bardsley et al.), samples each prompt ~90 times to build per-model focal distributions, computes a Coordination Index (probability two individuals pick the same option), and compares directly to human baselines, finding LLMs often outperform humans. The LessWrong post "Can LLMs Coordinate? A Simple Schelling Point Experiment" runs essentially the identical proposed protocol (5 independent frontier models, classic Schelling prompts like "a number between 1 and 10," meeting places, objects, measuring cross-model match rates), and the review "Schelling Coordination in LLMs: A Review" catalogues a whole prior literature (Poje 2024, Binder 2024, Motwani 2025, Järviniemi 2025) explicitly framing this as a multi-agent collusion / safety precondition. The only minor un-done piece is a single headline pairwise-cross-model-agreement-vs-human-baseline table, but all components already exist across these works.

evidence.title: Tacit Coordination of Large Language Models
evidence.summary: First large-scale assessment of LLM tacit coordination via the focal-point framework. Tests heterogeneous independent open-source models (Llama, Qwen, GPT-oss) on classic coordination games (Amsterdam/Nottingham, bargaining tables) drawn from Bardsley et al. human experiments, sampling ~90 times per question to build per-model focal distributions, computing a Coordination Index (probability two individuals choose the same strategy), and comparing to human baselines — finding LLMs often outperform humans but fail on numbers/cultural archetypes. Directly covers the proposal's problem and most of its method.

evidence.title: Can LLMs Coordinate? A Simple Schelling Point Experiment
evidence.summary: Runs essentially the proposed experiment: 5 independent models (GPT-5, Claude-4.5 Sonnet, Grok-4, Gemini-2.5-Pro, DeepSeek-R1) given 75 classic Schelling prompts (number 1-10, places, objects, words), measuring cross-model match rates. Finds strong convergence on concrete prompts (all pick '7', 'pond', 'Springfield'), weaker on abstract ones. Human baselines not included, but cross-model agreement is the central metric.

evidence.title: Schelling Coordination in LLMs: A Review
evidence.summary: Survey of the LLM-Schelling-coordination literature: Poje et al. 2024 (near-perfect heads/tails coordination), Binder et al. 2024 (~50% integer-selection agreement), Motwani et al. 2025 (covert shared encoding), Järviniemi 2025 (deployment-relevant coordination). Explicitly frames shared Schelling points as a precondition for multi-agent collusion and a threat to monitoring-based safety measures — the exact framing of the proposal.

evidence.title: LLMs as Strategic Actors: Behavioral Alignment, Risk Calibration, and Argumentation Framing in Geopolitical Simulations
evidence.summary: Measures inter-model vs human-model agreement, finding LLMs align marginally more strongly with one another (Krippendorff alpha 0.41) than with humans (0.39), attributed to shared training priors. Demonstrates the 'do models agree with each other more than with humans' question has already been answered affirmatively in a related setting.
